research_concepts: defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change
team-level trait reliability (split-half and season-to-season persistence)
regression to the mean in H2-H1 change
methodological_questions: What share of the variance in opponents' H2-H1 change is attributable to the defending team, versus opponent, game context and noise?
Does a defense's estimated effect persist across odd/even games within a season and across consecutive seasons?
How can the mechanical negative correlation between H1 level and H2-H1 change be removed?
What permutation null shows what reliability would arise with no real defense-specific effect?

historical_evidence.finding: First-half reliance on a play type did not predict second-half suppression after controlling for H1 PPP and mean reversion. Matched ATT did not survive BH adjustment (PNR ATT=+0.0313, BH_p=0.0658, WEAK; others NULL). Top-1 accuracy was 0.550 against a mean-reversion baseline of 0.511 (+0.039). The record says the bulk of H2 suppression is RTM. Recorded as an adequately powered null (B_powered_null), n=8873 team-games.

The apparent A1 adapter PPP lift failed falsification. Wrong-way teams did not do worse than no-signal teams, the gap did not widen with scheme-vote confidence, and next-game carryover was not supported (Welch t=-1.003, p=0.842). Recorded failure mechanism: construction, selection or labelling flaw, with limits from regression to the mean and label error.
Play-type PPP across playoff series game buckets showed no clear decline over a series (DRIVE 0.889 -> 0.949). The study was observational with selection caveats, no CIs and an unclear mechanism.

A first-half matchup ranking of counters beat continuing the suppressed play within the same game (BEST-AVOID +0.375 PO / +0.422 RS after correction). The record lists leakage as a limitation, and its corrected figures changed between versions. It concerns within-game counter selection, not team-level defensive traits.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting H2 suppression from H1 play-type usage beyond mean reversion
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null. Most of the apparent H2 suppression is regression to the mean (RTM_SELECTION).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating the adapter PPP lift as a real coverage response
failed_approaches.why: Artifact of construction, selection or labelling. The falsification tests (asymmetry, confidence gradient, carryover) did not support a real effect.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Pooled game-bucket PPP comparison as evidence of systematic change
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive. The design was observational with selection caveats and no CIs.

evidence_establishes: Earlier project work found that apparent H2 suppression or change is largely explained by regression to the mean (FAM:SF-APPS-070, rejected).
Apparent adaptation effects in this area have previously turned out to be construction or labelling artifacts (FAM:SF-APPA-001).
Without strict controls, H2-H1 style contrasts are vulnerable to RTM and selection.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is stable at the team level, whether across seasons or across split halves. No retrieved record estimated team-level reliability.
Whether any defense-specific variance component exists after adjusting for opponent, score state and RTM.
Whether the within-game counter result in FAM:SF03 says anything about a persistent defensive trait. It uses a different estimand.
own_inferences: Opponents' H2-H1 change is mechanically negatively correlated with opponents' H1 level. Without adjustment, any team-level 'effect' will partly reflect which opponents the team faced and their H1 outcomes.

Per-team-season noise is probably large relative to any true defense-specific H2-H1 effect, because games number only about 82-100 per team-season and game-level H2-H1 differences are noisy. Expected reliability is low, though this is an estimate rather than a measurement.
Roster turnover, coaching changes and schedule differences across seasons will further limit season-to-season persistence even if a within-season trait exists.
Given the prior RTM and artifact findings, a naive analysis would likely show some apparent persistence from schedule or opponent composition, so the null model must be built carefully.
uncertainties: The exact outcome metric is not specified (points, PPP, or efficiency change), nor how garbage time and overtime are handled.
The size of the true between-team variance is unknown, so power cannot be computed from the records.
It is unclear whether the 120 team-seasons are all regular-season data or include playoffs, which have tiny per-team samples.
The existing records are play-type focused, so how well they transfer to a team-level trait question is unclear.

historical_effect.explanation: The RTM-driven null (FAM:SF-APPS-070) and the artifact finding (FAM:SF-APPA-001) moved the decision from a plain proceed to proceed_with_changes. The changes are mandatory RTM and opponent adjustment, a permutation null and a variance-component framing. They also lowered the predicted probability of support. The records do not answer the team-trait question directly, so they did not justify a do_not_proceed.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 120 team-seasons (30 teams x 4 seasons) give about 90 consecutive-season pairs, so only moderate persistence can be detected. Within-season split-half reliability at the game level has more information.
H2-H1 difference scores are noisy, and any true defense-specific component is probably small relative to game-level noise.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests team-level reliability of defensive H2-H1 effects. Related work (FAM:SF-APPS-070, rejected) shows that H2 suppression is mostly RTM. FAM:SF-APPA-001 (artifact) shows that adaptation effects can come from construction flaws. FAM:SF-APPS-010 (inconclusive) found no clear within-series trend. FAM:SF03 (supported) is a within-game counter result, not a trait. The question is therefore only partly addressed and is open at the team-trait level.

risks.text: H2-H1 change is mechanically tied to the H1 level. Opponents' H1 outcomes must be modelled so that RTM is not read as a defensive effect.
A difference score has an inherent negative correlation with its baseline. The H1 baseline needs to be adjusted for, or H2 modelled with H1 as a covariate.
Opponent offensive quality, score state, blowout and garbage-time rest, pace, home/away, rest days and roster changes can all produce apparent team effects.
Difference scores have low reliability. The raw correlation will be attenuated, so reliability must be assessed with variance components and compared against a null.
There are few team-seasons, and playoff samples per team are tiny.
Roster, scheme and rule changes across seasons reduce persistence and confound it with real trait instability.
Several outcome definitions, time splits and subgroups would inflate false positives unless one primary specification is fixed.
The conclusion depends on the permutation null being correctly constructed, for example by keeping the opponent schedule and game structure fixed.

design.estimand: The defense-team variance component (ICC) in opponents' H2 minus expected H2 given the opponent's own H1 performance, opponent season strength, score state and venue. Secondary: the correlation of team defensive random effects between odd and even games within a season, and between consecutive seasons.
design.unit: Defending team-game for the variance component; team-season for persistence across seasons.
design.sample: All regular-season games from 2022-23 to 2025-26 (120 team-seasons) as primary, using the full 2025-26 data. Playoffs are excluded from the primary analysis and analysed only descriptively. Overtime is excluded or handled through regulation-time-only scoring, and garbage-time stretches are excluded by a fixed pre-declared margin rule.
design.power: Run a simulation before analysis using the observed game-level SD of H2-H1 outcomes and a grid of true team SDs, to find the smallest detectable variance component and persistence correlation. With about 90 consecutive-season pairs, the persistence correlation has a standard error of roughly 0.10, so only moderate persistence is detectable. The primary reliability test uses within-season odd/even game splits, which have more information.
design.controls: Mixed model with random effects for defending team and offensive team, fixed effects for opponent H1 performance, home/away, rest days, pace and season, and a score-state adjustment. Compare against H2 modelled directly with H1 as a covariate rather than the raw difference.
design.falsification: A permutation null that shuffles defense labels within opponent-season strata, preserving schedule structure. A placebo using a different split, such as Q1-Q2 vs Q3-Q4 or random game halves, should show no defense-specific effect beyond the general defensive trait. Compare against general defensive rating persistence to test whether H2-H1 adds anything beyond it. Also run a negative control with the offensive side.
design.multiplicity: One pre-registered primary metric (points per 100 possessions, regular season) and one primary reliability statistic (the odd/even variance component with a 95% bootstrap CI over games). Secondary analyses are labelled exploratory and BH-adjusted.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the defense variance component CI excludes zero, the observed value exceeds the 95th percentile of the permutation null, and the between-season persistence is positive with a CI excluding zero. If the CI excludes any practically meaningful size and the upper bound is below the pre-set threshold (ICC under 0.05), conclude rejected. Otherwise report uncertain.
design.data_version: Data as available on 2026-10-06: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 per-game files, with 2025-26 regular season and playoffs complete. Freeze the data extract and record its version hash before analysis.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half change
methodological_questions: Is the defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons (split-half or season-to-season correlation)?
How much of the team-level variance is noise versus signal given 120 team-seasons?
How to control for regression to the mean, score-state/garbage-time confounding, and opponent strength?
Is there a placebo or null distribution (e.g., permuted opponents) for the trait?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

reasoning_details.text:
I'm wrapping up now and may not need any more tools. The records I pulled up are SF-APPS-070, which was rejected, SF-APPA-001, which is an artifact, SF-APPS-010, which is inconclusive, and SF03, which is supported but only about same-game counters rather than a team trait. None of them speak directly to whether the defensive effect is reliable at the team level.

I'm now working out how to measure whether the defensive effect holds at the team level, using an intraclass correlation adjusted for regression to the mean and opponent strength. The plan is a split-half and season-to-season check with a mixed model and a permutation null, with my own estimate that the true effect variance is very small.

I'm checking the variance estimate against the team-season count, which looks sufficient for a component model across 30 teams. Next I'm noting the data cutoff, the roster changes across seasons, and the garbage-time and overtime exclusions. I also need to watch for a mechanical negative correlation between the first-half level and the half-to-half change, plus blowouts, starters resting, and possible pace effects.
